```{ojs}
Plot = require("@observablehq/plot@0.6.16")
d3 = require("d3@7.9.0")
topo = require("topojson-client@3.1.0")
bzOrder = (q, n) => {
  let h = 0;
  for (const ch of q) h = (h * 31 + ch.charCodeAt(0)) >>> 0;
  return d3.shuffler(d3.randomLcg((h % 10000) / 10000))(d3.range(n));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Inline check builder: a button that opens a short multiple-choice check with instant feedback.
bzCheck = function(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" class="bz-check" style="margin:14px 0 24px 0;text-align:center;">
    <button class="bz-check-toggle" style="display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1d4ed8 0%,#0891b2 100%);color:#fff;border:none;padding:10px 22px;min-height:44px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.95em;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;box-shadow:0 3px 12px rgba(29,78,216,.4);">
      <span>📝</span> ${title} <span class="chevron" style="transition:transform .3s;">▼</span>
    </button>
    <div class="quiz-body" style="max-height:0;opacity:0;overflow:hidden;transition:max-height .5s ease,opacity .4s ease;margin-top:0;text-align:left;"></div>
  </div>`;
  const toggle = outer.querySelector("button");
  const chevron = toggle.querySelector(".chevron");
  const body = outer.querySelector(".quiz-body");
  let open = false;
  toggle.onclick = () => {
    open = !open;
    body.style.maxHeight = open ? "4000px" : "0";
    body.style.opacity = open ? "1" : "0";
    body.style.marginTop = open ? "14px" : "0";
    chevron.style.transform = open ? "rotate(180deg)" : "rotate(0)";
  };
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:14px 18px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.1);border:1px solid #e2e8f0;";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;">${qi + 1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.92em;";
    const order = bzOrder(qq.q, qq.options.length);
    const shownCorrect = order.indexOf(qq.correct);
    order.map(i => qq.options[i]).forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.className = "bz-opt";
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        const btns = card.querySelectorAll("button");
        btns.forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; });
        btns[shownCorrect].style.borderColor = "#48bb78"; btns[shownCorrect].style.background = "#f0fff4";
        if (oi === shownCorrect) {
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#276749"; fb.style.background = "#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor = "#fc8181"; btn.style.background = "#fff5f5";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ Not quite. " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; fb.style.background = "#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding = "10px 14px"; fb.style.marginTop = "8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  return outer;
}
```

# Engage: Winter Storm Jonas {#bz-engage}

::: {.engage-box}
## ❄️ January 22–24, 2016: The Storm That Shut Down New York

**Investigative phenomenon:** *Winter Storm Jonas produced strong enough winds and enough snow to cause significant disruptions to society, damage to property, and harm to human life.*

- 📏 **27.5 inches** of snow in Central Park, the **biggest single snowstorm** there since records began in 1869
- 🚫 New York City **banned driving** on January 23, and subways above ground stopped
- 💨 Strong winds blew the snow into drifts and caused **coastal flooding** along the Mid-Atlantic and Long Island shores
- 😢 Dozens of deaths across the eastern U.S., many from car accidents, shoveling, and cold

**To explain a blizzard, we need to explain two things: the WIND and the SNOW.** We'll start with wind.
:::

In class you watch the video *Winter Storm Jonas in NYC*. Here is how big this one storm was compared with a whole winter in NYC:

# Explore 1: Wind Formation Investigation {#bz-explore-1}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🔬 Why Does Air Move?

Wind is moving air. In this investigation you use **three models** to find cause-and-effect links between **temperature, density, pressure, and rising or sinking air (buoyancy)**. First, a warm-up about how air changes as you go up.
:::

## Atmospheric Sciences: Felix Baumgartner's Jump {#bz-felix}

On **October 14, 2012**, Felix Baumgartner rode a helium balloon to about **39 km (127,852 ft)** above New Mexico and jumped. He fell faster than the speed of sound, reaching about **1,358 km/h (844 mph, Mach 1.25)**. At launch the balloon was a tall, skinny bubble with most of its plastic hanging empty. High up, it had swelled into a giant sphere.

Slide up through the atmosphere to see why. Values are from the U.S. Standard Atmosphere.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzAtm = [
  {km: 0, hPa: 1013.25, rho: 1.225, K: 288.15}, {km: 5, hPa: 540.5, rho: 0.7364, K: 255.65},
  {km: 10, hPa: 265.0, rho: 0.4135, K: 223.15}, {km: 15, hPa: 121.1, rho: 0.1948, K: 216.65},
  {km: 20, hPa: 55.29, rho: 0.08891, K: 216.65}, {km: 25, hPa: 25.49, rho: 0.04008, K: 221.65},
  {km: 30, hPa: 11.97, rho: 0.01841, K: 226.65}, {km: 35, hPa: 5.746, rho: 0.008463, K: 236.65},
  {km: 40, hPa: 2.871, rho: 0.003996, K: 250.35}
]
bzAtmAt = (km) => {
  const i = Math.min(bzAtm.length - 2, Math.floor(km / 5));
  const a = bzAtm[i], b = bzAtm[i + 1], f = (km - a.km) / 5;
  const lerpLog = (x, y) => Math.exp(Math.log(x) + f * (Math.log(y) - Math.log(x)));
  return {km, hPa: lerpLog(a.hPa, b.hPa), rho: lerpLog(a.rho, b.rho), K: a.K + f * (b.K - a.K)};
}
viewof bzAlt = Inputs.range([0, 39], {step: 0.5, value: 0, label: "Altitude (km)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const s = bzAtmAt(bzAlt), s0 = bzAtm[0];
  const vol = (s.K / s.hPa) / (s0.K / s0.hPa);
  const pct = 100 * s.hPa / s0.hPa;
  const r = Math.min(70, 14 * Math.cbrt(vol));
  const card = html`<div class="bz-card" style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:14px;align-items:center;">
    <svg viewBox="0 0 160 170" width="150" height="160" role="img" aria-label="Balloon size at this altitude">
      <rect x="0" y="0" width="160" height="170" fill="${d3.interpolateRgb("#bfdbfe", "#0f172a")(Math.min(1, bzAlt / 39))}" rx="10"/>
      <ellipse cx="80" cy="${85 - r * 0.2}" rx="${r}" ry="${Math.max(r, 18)}" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#64748b"/>
      <line x1="80" y1="${85 - r * 0.2 + Math.max(r, 18)}" x2="80" y2="160" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>
      <rect x="72" y="152" width="16" height="12" fill="#f59e0b"/>
    </svg>
    <div style="flex:1 1 200px;line-height:1.7;">
      <div><b>Altitude:</b> ${bzAlt} km</div>
      <div><b>Air pressure:</b> ${s.hPa.toFixed(s.hPa < 10 ? 1 : 0)} hPa (${pct < 1 ? pct.toFixed(2) : pct.toFixed(0)}% of sea level)</div>
      <div><b>Air density:</b> ${s.rho < 0.01 ? s.rho.toFixed(4) : s.rho.toFixed(3)} kg/m³</div>
      <div><b>Same helium would fill:</b> ${vol.toFixed(vol < 10 ? 1 : 0)}× its ground volume</div>
      <div><b>Air resistance at the same speed:</b> ${(100 * s.rho / s0.rho).toFixed(s.rho / s0.rho < 0.1 ? 1 : 0)}% of sea level</div>
    </div></div>`;
  return card;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzCheck("bz-check-felix", "Check: The packet's three questions", [
  {q: "Question 1: No gas was added after launch. Why did the balloon get so much bigger?",
   options: ["The Sun heated the helium until it boiled", "Outside air pressure dropped with altitude, so fewer air molecules pushed on the balloon and the helium spread out (expanded)", "The balloon absorbed water vapor", "Gravity is weaker at 39 km, so the balloon stretched"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "At 39 km the air pressure is less than 1% of sea level. With so little air pushing in, the helium molecules spread apart and the balloon swelled to well over 100 times its ground volume."},
  {q: "Question 2: Why couldn't Felix keep going about 800 mph as he fell lower?",
   options: ["He ran out of fuel", "Lower down the air is much denser, so more air molecules pushed against him (more air resistance) and slowed him", "Gravity gets weaker near the ground", "The Earth's rotation slowed him"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Near 39 km the air is about 0.3% as dense as at sea level, so there is almost nothing to slow him. As he fell into thicker air, air resistance grew and his speed dropped."},
  {q: "Question 3: Why did Felix first feel he was 'hauling' only when he was going about 600 mph slower than his top speed?",
   options: ["He couldn't see the ground", "Up high there were so few air molecules that he couldn't feel or hear air rushing past; lower down, the dense air pushed on him and he could feel the speed", "His suit was broken", "Sound travels faster up high"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "We feel speed through air hitting us. Thin air = few molecules = little push. This shows that the number of air molecules in a space (density) changes a lot from place to place, which matters for wind."}
])
```

## Model 1: Wind Formation {#bz-model-1}

In class you connect two 1-liter bottles with a tube. One bottle has **hot water** ("very warm land") and one has **cold water** ("very cool land"). Smoke from an incense stick shows how the air moves (the incense does **not** heat the air). Try the virtual version: choose where to hold the incense and press **Run**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bzBottleStart = Inputs.radio(["Cold-water bottle", "Hot-water bottle"], {label: "Hold the smoking incense in the:", value: "Cold-water bottle"})
```

```{ojs}

{
  const W = 380, H = 300;

  wrap.append(canvas, html`<div></div>`, runBtn, note);
  const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
  const L = {x0: 40, x1: 160}, R = {x0: 220, x1: 340}, top = 60, water = 230, tubeY0 = 200, tubeY1 = 220;
  const coldLeft = true;
  let parts = [], t = 0, running = false, raf;
  const inCold = bzBottleStart === "Cold-water bottle";
  function draw() {
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#f8fafc"; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);
    // water
    ctx.fillStyle = "#93c5fd"; ctx.fillRect(L.x0, water, L.x1 - L.x0, 50);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#fca5a5"; ctx.fillRect(R.x0, water, R.x1 - R.x0, 50);
    // bottles
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#334155"; ctx.lineWidth = 2;
    for (const B of [L, R]) {
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(B.x0, 280); ctx.lineTo(B.x0, top + 30); ctx.lineTo((B.x0 + B.x1) / 2 - 12, top); ctx.lineTo((B.x0 + B.x1) / 2 - 12, top - 22);
      ctx.moveTo((B.x0 + B.x1) / 2 + 12, top - 22); ctx.lineTo((B.x0 + B.x1) / 2 + 12, top); ctx.lineTo(B.x1, top + 30); ctx.lineTo(B.x1, 280); ctx.lineTo(B.x0, 280);
      ctx.stroke();
    }
    // tube
    ctx.fillStyle = "#e2e8f0"; ctx.fillRect(L.x1, tubeY0, R.x0 - L.x1, tubeY1 - tubeY0);
    ctx.strokeRect(L.x1, tubeY0, R.x0 - L.x1, tubeY1 - tubeY0);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#1e293b"; ctx.font = "bold 12px sans-serif"; ctx.textAlign = "center";
    ctx.fillText("Cold water", (L.x0 + L.x1) / 2, 262); ctx.fillText("(very cool land)", (L.x0 + L.x1) / 2, 276);
    ctx.fillText("Hot water", (R.x0 + R.x1) / 2, 262); ctx.fillText("(very warm land)", (R.x0 + R.x1) / 2, 276);
    // smoke
    for (const p of parts) {
      ctx.fillStyle = `rgba(71,85,105,${Math.max(0.15, 0.7 - p.age / 1400)})`;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(p.x, p.y, 3.2, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill();
    }
    // incense
    if (running && t < 900) {
      const ix = inCold ? (L.x0 + L.x1) / 2 : (R.x0 + R.x1) / 2;
      ctx.strokeStyle = "#92400e"; ctx.lineWidth = 3; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(ix, 20); ctx.lineTo(ix, 205); ctx.stroke();
    }
  }
  function step() {
    t++;
    if (t < 900 && t % 3 === 0) {
      const ix = inCold ? (L.x0 + L.x1) / 2 : (R.x0 + R.x1) / 2;
      parts.push({x: ix + (Math.random() - .5) * 6, y: 205, age: 0});
    }
    for (const p of parts) {
      p.age++;
      const jx = (Math.random() - .5) * 1.2, jy = (Math.random() - .5) * 1.2;
      if (p.x < L.x1) { // cold bottle: sink, then drift toward the tube
        if (p.y < water - 14) { p.y += 0.55 + jy; p.x += jx; }
        else { p.y += jy * 0.5; p.x += 0.6 + jx; if (p.y > water - 4) p.y = water - 4; }
        if (p.x >= L.x1 - 2 && (p.y < tubeY0 + 2 || p.y > tubeY1 - 2)) { p.y = tubeY0 + 3 + Math.random() * (tubeY1 - tubeY0 - 6); }
      } else if (p.x < R.x0) { // in the tube: flow toward the warm side
        p.x += 1.0; p.y = Math.min(tubeY1 - 3, Math.max(tubeY0 + 3, p.y + jy * 0.4));
      } else { // warm bottle: rise
        if (p.y > top + 34) { p.y -= 0.75 + Math.random() * 0.3; p.x += jx * 1.6; }
        else { p.x += jx * 2; p.y += jy; }
      }
      p.x = Math.min(R.x1 - 4, Math.max(L.x0 + 4, p.x));
      if (p.x > L.x1 - 1 && p.x < R.x0 + 1 && (p.y < tubeY0 || p.y > tubeY1)) p.x = p.x < (L.x1 + R.x0) / 2 ? L.x1 - 3 : R.x0 + 3;
      p.y = Math.max(top + 8, Math.min(water - 3, p.y));
    }
    draw();
    if (t > 1500) { running = false; note.textContent = inCold ? "Smoke sank in the cold bottle, flowed through the tube along the 'surface,' and rose in the hot bottle." : "Smoke rose straight up in the hot bottle and stayed near the top. Almost none moved through the tube."; return; }
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  }
  runBtn.onclick = () => { cancelAnimationFrame(raf); parts = []; t = 0; running = true; note.textContent = "Watching..."; step(); };
  draw();
  invalidation.then(() => cancelAnimationFrame(raf));
  return wrap;
}
```

<p class="bz-note">This is a model of what students observe in the bottle lab (sped up). The motion follows the teacher guide's expected observations, not a fluid-dynamics calculation.</p>

## Model 2: What effect does heating and cooling have on air molecules? {#bz-model-2}

Heat energy from Earth's surface is transferred to the air above it. In class you use the PhET **States of Matter** simulator (States → Oxygen → Gas) and cool and heat the gas between about **80 K and 200 K**. This virtual version is a column of oxygen molecules sitting on "Earth's surface," pulled down by gravity. Change the temperature and watch the molecules near the surface.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bzT2 = Inputs.range([80, 200], {step: 10, value: 140, label: "Temperature (K)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzCol = {
  const W = 300, H = 280, N = 150, g = 0.15;
  const sigmaAt = T => 5.9 * Math.sqrt(T / 200);
  const wrap = html`<div class="bz-card" style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:14px;align-items:flex-start;"></div>`;
  const canvas = DOM.canvas(W, H);
  canvas.style.width = "100%"; canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; canvas.style.height = "auto";
  const stats = html`<div style="flex:1 1 180px;line-height:1.8;font-size:.95em;"></div>`;
  wrap.append(canvas, stats);
  const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
  const s0 = sigmaAt(140);
  const P = d3.range(N).map(() => ({x: Math.random() * W, y: H - Math.random() * H * 0.4, vx: d3.randomNormal(0, s0)(), vy: d3.randomNormal(0, s0)()}));
  let T = 140, raf, frame = 0, hits = 0, hitHist = [];
  const state = {setT(newT) { const f = Math.sqrt(newT / T); for (const p of P) { p.vx *= f; p.vy *= f; } T = newT; }};
  function tick() {
    frame++; let h = 0;
    for (const p of P) {
      p.vy += g; p.x += p.vx; p.y += p.vy;
      if (p.x < 3) { p.x = 3; p.vx = Math.abs(p.vx); }
      if (p.x > W - 3) { p.x = W - 3; p.vx = -Math.abs(p.vx); }
      if (p.y > H - 3) { p.y = H - 3; h += Math.abs(p.vy); p.vy = -Math.abs(p.vy); }
      if (p.y < 3) { p.y = 3; p.vy = Math.abs(p.vy); }
    }
    hitHist.push(h); if (hitHist.length > 120) hitHist.shift();
    ctx.fillStyle = "#eff6ff"; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.fillStyle = "rgba(34,197,94,.18)"; ctx.fillRect(0, H * 0.8, W, H * 0.2);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#166534"; ctx.font = "11px sans-serif"; ctx.fillText("Air near Earth's surface (bottom fifth)", 6, H * 0.8 + 13);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#15803d"; ctx.fillRect(0, H - 3, W, 3);
    const col = d3.interpolateRgb("#2563eb", "#dc2626")((T - 80) / 120);
    ctx.fillStyle = col;
    for (const p of P) { ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(p.x, p.y, 3.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill(); }
    if (frame % 10 === 0) {
      const near = P.filter(p => p.y > H * 0.8).length;
      const avgH = d3.mean(P, p => H - p.y);
      stats.innerHTML = `<div><b>Temperature:</b> ${T} K</div>
        <div><b>Molecules near the surface:</b> ${near} of ${N}</div>
        <div><b>Average height of molecules:</b> ${Math.round(100 * avgH / H)}% of the column</div>
        <div><b>Average speed:</b> ${(Math.sqrt(T / 200) * 100).toFixed(0)}% of the speed at 200 K</div>
        <div style="font-size:.85em;opacity:.8;margin-top:6px;">Molecules are oxygen (O₂). Only gravity and bounces off the walls act on them in this model.</div>`;
    }
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  }
  tick();
  invalidation.then(() => cancelAnimationFrame(raf));
  wrap.value = state;
  return wrap;
}
```

### ✏️ In your packet: Model 2 See-Think-Wonder (pp. 6–7)

For **cooling** and **heating**, describe what happens to the **air molecules**, their **density** at "Earth's surface," and the **pressure** they apply on "Earth's surface." For each, write what it makes you think about the air in the bottles.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔎 What about pressure?
Air pressure at the surface comes from air molecules pushing on it. In the real atmosphere, **cool, dense air sinks and piles up**, so more air presses on the surface there: **higher pressure**. Over warm land, the air **expands and rises** and some of it flows away up high, so less air presses down: **lower pressure**. The teacher guide's expected idea: *"When air molecules were warmed and spread apart and rose up there was less pressure on 'Earth's surface'; when they were cooled and came closer together there was more pressure."*
:::

## Model 3: What causes movement of air across Earth's surface? {#bz-model-3}

Now we recreate Model 1 at the **particle level**, like the packet's **Diffusion Simulator**. The packet's settings: **left side 200 particles at 250 K** (like the cool-land bottle) and **right side 50 particles at 300 K** (like the warm-land bottle). Mass (28 AMU) and radius stay the same, because air molecules are about the same everywhere. Predict what will happen when you remove the divider, then test it.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bzDiffSet = Inputs.form({
  nL: Inputs.range([10, 250], {step: 10, value: 200, label: "Left: number of particles"}),
  tL: Inputs.range([100, 400], {step: 10, value: 250, label: "Left: temperature (K)"}),
  nR: Inputs.range([10, 250], {step: 10, value: 50, label: "Right: number of particles"}),
  tR: Inputs.range([100, 400], {step: 10, value: 300, label: "Right: temperature (K)"})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 340, H = 220, mid = W / 2;
  const {nL, tL, nR, tR} = bzDiffSet;
  const sp = T => 1.6 * Math.sqrt(T / 300);
  const mk = (n, T, x0, x1, side) => d3.range(n).map(() => { const a = Math.random() * 2 * Math.PI, s = sp(T) * (0.6 + Math.random() * 0.8); return {x: x0 + 4 + Math.random() * (x1 - x0 - 8), y: 4 + Math.random() * (H - 8), vx: s * Math.cos(a), vy: s * Math.sin(a), side}; });
  const P = [...mk(nL, tL, 0, mid, "L"), ...mk(nR, tR, mid, W, "R")];
  let divider = true, raf, frame = 0, crossLR = 0, crossRL = 0;
  const wrap = html`<div class="bz-card"></div>`;
  const canvas = DOM.canvas(W, H);
  canvas.style.width = "100%"; canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; canvas.style.height = "auto";
  const btn = html`<button class="bz-btn">Remove divider</button>`;
  const stats = html`<div style="font-size:.93em;line-height:1.7;margin-top:6px;"></div>`;
  wrap.append(canvas, html`<div></div>`, btn, stats);
  const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
  btn.onclick = () => { divider = !divider; btn.textContent = divider ? "Remove divider" : "Put divider back"; };
  function tick() {
    frame++;
    for (const p of P) {
      const wasLeft = p.x < mid;
      p.x += p.vx; p.y += p.vy;
      if (p.x < 3) { p.x = 3; p.vx = Math.abs(p.vx); }
      if (p.x > W - 3) { p.x = W - 3; p.vx = -Math.abs(p.vx); }
      if (p.y < 3) { p.y = 3; p.vy = Math.abs(p.vy); }
      if (p.y > H - 3) { p.y = H - 3; p.vy = -Math.abs(p.vy); }
      if (divider) {
        if (wasLeft && p.x >= mid - 3) { p.x = mid - 3; p.vx = -Math.abs(p.vx); }
        if (!wasLeft && p.x <= mid + 3) { p.x = mid + 3; p.vx = Math.abs(p.vx); }
      } else {
        if (wasLeft && p.x >= mid) crossLR++;
        if (!wasLeft && p.x < mid) crossRL++;
      }
    }
    ctx.fillStyle = "#f8fafc"; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);
    for (const p of P) { ctx.fillStyle = p.side === "L" ? "#2563eb" : "#dc2626"; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(p.x, p.y, 2.6, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill(); }
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#334155"; ctx.lineWidth = 2; ctx.strokeRect(1, 1, W - 2, H - 2);
    if (divider) { ctx.fillStyle = "#334155"; ctx.fillRect(mid - 2, 0, 4, H); }
    if (frame % 10 === 0) {
      const inL = P.filter(p => p.x < mid), inR = P.filter(p => p.x >= mid);
      const pres = arr => d3.sum(arr, p => p.vx * p.vx + p.vy * p.vy);
      const pL = pres(inL), pR = pres(inR), pMax = Math.max(pL, pR, 1);
      stats.innerHTML = `<div><b>Particles:</b> left ${inL.length} | right ${inR.length}</div>
        <div><b>Pressure</b> (how hard particles push on the walls):</div>
        <div style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:6px;"><span style="width:44px;">Left</span><div style="height:14px;width:${Math.round(180 * pL / pMax)}px;background:#2563eb;border-radius:4px;"></div></div>
        <div style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:6px;"><span style="width:44px;">Right</span><div style="height:14px;width:${Math.round(180 * pR / pMax)}px;background:#dc2626;border-radius:4px;"></div></div>
        ${divider ? "" : `<div><b>Crossed left → right:</b> ${crossLR} &nbsp; <b>right → left:</b> ${crossRL}</div>`}`;
    }
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  }
  tick();
  invalidation.then(() => cancelAnimationFrame(raf));
  return wrap;
}
```

<p class="bz-note">Blue = particles that started on the left (cool, crowded side). Red = started on the right (warm, less crowded side). Pressure here is an ideal gas: it grows with the number of particles and with their speed (temperature). With the packet's settings, the left side's pressure is about 3 times the right side's (200 × 250 vs. 50 × 300).</p>

## Making Sense of the Wind Formation Investigation {#bz-making-sense-1}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

The teacher guide lists these as the ideas you need for Explain 1:

- **Model 1:** Air over the "cool land" sinks. Air over the "warm land" rises. Air moves from the "cool land" side to the "warm land" side.
- **Model 2:** Cooled air molecules come closer together, so the air is **more dense**. Warmed molecules move farther apart, so the air is **less dense**. Warmed molecules spread apart and rise, so there's **less pressure** on Earth's surface; cooled molecules crowd together at the surface, so there's **more pressure**.
- **Model 3:** Most molecules flow from the **cooler, denser** side to the **warmer, less dense** side, because there are more molecules and more pressure on the cool side and more room on the other side.
:::

# Explain 1: Explaining Wind Formation {#bz-explain-1}

::: {.explain-box}
## 🧠 From Molecules to Wind

Now use the molecule-scale evidence to explain a big, observable thing: **wind**. You'll answer two questions: *What causes air to sink or rise?* and *Why would air molecules move horizontally to create wind?*
:::

## Movement of Air Molecules Due to Pressure Differences {#bz-pressure-containers}

Each container has two sides separated by a wall. The dots are air molecules.

## What caused the rising and sinking, and the sideways flow, in the bottles? {#bz-bottles}

Step through the explanation. This is what your drawings on pp. 11–12 should show.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bzBotStep = Inputs.radio(["1. Heating and cooling", "2. Rising and sinking", "3. Pressure", "4. Sideways flow (wind)"], {value: "1. Heating and cooling", label: "Step:"})
```

```{ojs}

{
  const s = +bzBotStep[0];
  const rnd = d3.randomLcg(0.42);
  const dotsIn = (x0, n, spread) => d3.range(n).map(() => ({x: x0 + 10 + rnd() * 100, y: 230 - (spread ? rnd() * 150 : rnd() * 80)}));
  const cold = dotsIn(40, 34, false), warm = dotsIn(220, 14, true);
  const arrow = (x1, y1, x2, y2, c) => `<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="${c}" stroke-width="4" marker-end="url(#bzah-${c.slice(1)})"/>`;
  const txt = [

    <rect x="220" y="240" width="120" height="40" fill="#fca5a5" stroke="#334155"/><text x="280" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">Very warm land</text>
    <rect x="160" y="212" width="60" height="20" fill="#e2e8f0" stroke="#334155"/>

    ${warm.map(d => `<circle cx="${d.x.toFixed(1)}" cy="${d.y.toFixed(1)}" r="3.4" fill="#dc2626"/>`).join("")}
```

<p class="bz-note">In the bottle model, "H" and "L" are the pressures near the surface (the water). In the real atmosphere the air that rises over warm land spreads out and flows back toward the cool side high up, which keeps the circulation going.</p>

## Explaining Wind from Winter Storm Jonas {#bz-jonas-wind}

**Prompt: What causes the wind from Winter Storm Jonas to occur?** The packet's diagram shows the **troposphere** over land that is cooler on one side and warmer on the other. Change the temperature difference between the two land areas and watch what happens to the pressure difference and the wind.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bzDeltaT = Inputs.range([0, 30], {step: 1, value: 15, label: "Temperature difference between the land areas (°C)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const k = bzDeltaT / 30;
  const wArrow = 1 + 9 * k;
  const nCold = Math.round(20 + 14 * k), nWarm = Math.round(20 - 10 * k);
  const rnd = d3.randomLcg(0.9);
  const box = (x0, n) => d3.range(n).map(() => `<circle cx="${(x0 + 4 + rnd() * 52).toFixed(1)}" cy="${(232 + rnd() * 42).toFixed(1)}" r="2.5" fill="#1e293b"/>`).join("");
  const label = bzDeltaT === 0 ? "No temperature difference → no pressure difference → no wind." :
    bzDeltaT < 10 ? "Small temperature difference → small pressure difference → light wind." :
    bzDeltaT < 20 ? "Bigger temperature difference → bigger pressure difference → stronger wind." :
    "Large temperature difference → large pressure difference → strong wind, like Jonas.";
  return html`<div class="bz-card">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 400 290" width="100%" style="max-width:520px;display:block;margin:auto;" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of the troposphere: cool sinking air and high pressure over cool land on the left, warm rising air and low pressure over warm land on the right, with wind blowing along the surface from high to low">
    <defs><marker id="bzw" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="3.2" markerHeight="3.2" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#475569"/></marker>
    <marker id="bzwb" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="3.2" markerHeight="3.2" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#2563eb"/></marker>
    <marker id="bzwr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="3.2" markerHeight="3.2" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#dc2626"/></marker></defs>
    <path d="M10,60 Q200,20 390,60" fill="none" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-dasharray="5,4"/>
    <text x="200" y="28" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#475569">Upper troposphere = cool</text>
    <path d="M10,200 Q200,175 390,200" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="6"/>
    <text x="200" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#166534">Earth's surface</text>
    <line x1="80" y1="80" x2="80" y2="${170 - 0}" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="${2 + 4 * k}" marker-end="url(#bzwb)"/>
    <text x="80" y="72" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1d4ed8" font-weight="bold">Cool sinking air</text>
    <line x1="320" y1="170" x2="320" y2="80" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="${2 + 4 * k}" marker-end="url(#bzwr)"/>
    <text x="320" y="72" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#b91c1c" font-weight="bold">Warm rising air</text>
    <text x="104" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="${16 + 8 * k}" font-weight="bold" fill="#1d4ed8" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke">H</text>
    <text x="296" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="${16 + 8 * k}" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke">L</text>
    ${bzDeltaT > 0 ? `<line x1="110" y1="182" x2="290" y2="182" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="${wArrow}" marker-end="url(#bzw)"/>
    <line x1="290" y1="95" x2="110" y2="95" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="${Math.max(1, wArrow / 2)}" stroke-dasharray="6,4" marker-end="url(#bzw)"/>` : ""}
    <text x="200" y="170" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#334155">${bzDeltaT > 0 ? "WIND" : ""}</text>
    <rect x="50" y="228" width="60" height="50" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#334155"/><text x="80" y="288" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1e293b">Land is cooler here</text>
    <rect x="290" y="228" width="60" height="50" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#334155"/><text x="320" y="288" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1e293b">Land is warmer here</text>

```

<p class="bz-note">The boxes show air molecules near the surface (more crowded = denser = higher pressure). The dashed arrow is the return flow high up. Arrow thickness is a qualitative picture of "more" or "less," not a calculated wind speed.</p>

::: {.key-idea}
### 💡 Consensus ideas (Take Time for These Key Points)
- **High pressure** at Earth's surface is where **cold air contracts**, is **more dense**, and **sinks**.
- **Low pressure** at Earth's surface is where **warm air expands**, is **less dense**, and **rises**. Air converges there and is forced up.
- Air moves **horizontally** across Earth's surface because of **differences in air pressure**: from **high to low**, because there is more space for molecules to flow into where pressure is low.
- This is how the wind from Winter Storm Jonas formed, and how wind from other storms like it forms.
:::

### Making a causal claim: independent and dependent variables {#bz-variables}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzCheck("bz-check-variables", "Check: Variables in the wind model", [
  {q: "In the wind model, what is the DEPENDENT variable (the effect)?",
   options: ["The temperature of the land", "The wind (its speed and direction across the surface)", "The Sun", "The tube"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Wind depends on other parts of the system (the pressure difference, which depends on heating and cooling). It is the effect."},
  {q: "What is the INDEPENDENT variable (the cause that drives the change)?",
   options: ["The wind speed", "The difference in temperature (uneven heating and cooling) of Earth's surface", "The number of clouds", "The direction of the arrows"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Uneven heating makes density differences, which make pressure differences, which make wind. The temperature difference drives everything else in the model."},
  {q: "Which statement best states the relationship?",
   options: ["The more wind there is, the warmer the land gets", "The greater the temperature difference between two areas, the greater the pressure difference, and the stronger the wind blowing from high to low pressure", "Temperature has no effect on wind", "Wind always blows from warm to cool areas along the surface"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "That's a cause-and-effect claim you can use to make predictions about future storms. Surface wind blows from the cool, high-pressure side toward the warm, low-pressure side."}
])
```

Revisit your Engage ideas. Which ones can you **keep**, **change**, or **cross off**?

```{ojs}

{
  const verdict = {
    "Wind is when air moves from one place to another fast": "✅ Keep: wind is air moving horizontally across Earth's surface.",
    "Wind is somehow caused by temperature changes": "✅ Keep and add detail: uneven heating → density differences → pressure differences → wind.",
    "Wind has to do with air pressure": "✅ Keep: air moves from high to low pressure.",
    "Wind is caused by the Earth spinning": "✏️ Change: Earth's spin doesn't start the wind, but it does turn wind's direction (you'll see wind circling highs and lows in the Elaborate).",
    "Wind is caused by clouds or snow pushing the air": "❌ Cross off: clouds and snow form in the same storm, but pressure differences drive the wind.",
    "Trees moving make the wind": "❌ Cross off: trees move because of the wind, not the other way around."
  };
  if (!bzIdeas.length) return html`<p class="bz-note">You didn't pick any ideas in the Engage. Scroll up and choose some to see feedback here.</p>`;
  return html`<div class="bz-card"><ul style="margin:0;padding-left:18px;">${bzIdeas.map(i => html`<li style="margin:4px 0;"><b>${i}</b><br>${verdict[i]}</li>`)}</ul></div>`;
```

### Summary Task {#bz-summary-1}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Summary Task (p. 16)

1. How have we used **mechanisms at a molecular scale** to figure out what causes wind to move across Earth's surface?
2. How did your model of wind formation show how **energy and matter interact** within the storm system, at a large observable scale and at a molecular scale?
3. Claims about variables: (a) How did you identify the independent and dependent variable? (b) In your own words, how did you decide which was which?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Summary Task (try it first!)
1. **Molecular scale → wind:** Heating gives air molecules more energy, so they move faster and spread apart (less dense, rises). Cooling slows them and packs them together (denser, sinks). Crowded molecules at the surface = high pressure; spread-out molecules = low pressure. More molecules move from high to low pressure, and that net movement is wind.
2. **Energy and matter:** *Energy* (heat from the land) flows into the air and changes molecule speed. *Matter* (the air itself) moves in a loop: it sinks over cool land, flows along the surface from H to L, rises over warm land, and returns high up. Observable scale: smoke and wind. Molecular scale: molecule speed and spacing.
3. **Variables:** The dependent variable is the thing that **changes because of** something else (wind). The independent variable **drives** the change and doesn't depend on the other parts of the model (temperature difference from uneven heating). A test: "Does A change B, or does B change A?" Heating changes the wind; the wind doesn't decide how hot the land is.
:::

# Explore 2: Precipitation Formation Investigation {#bz-explore-2}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🌧️ Where Does All That Snow Come From?

Jonas didn't just blow; it dumped **27.5 inches** of snow on Central Park. Think of a really muggy, humid day: how could you tell the air was full of water? In this investigation you use models of **fronts** and **cloud formation** to find out how water moves through the atmosphere and why precipitation happens where air masses meet.
:::

## Model 1: Air Masses and Their Interactions {#bz-fronts}

Air varies in temperature and moisture. A huge body of air with about the same temperature and moisture throughout is an **air mass**. When a relatively **cold, dry** air mass meets a relatively **warm, moist** air mass, the boundary between them is a **front**. Play the simulator for each of the **four types of fronts**: cold, warm, occluded, and stationary.

```{=html}
<iframe class="bz-frame" src="weatherfronts.html" title="Weather Fronts Simulation" loading="lazy" style="height: 980px;"></iframe>
```

<p class="bz-note">If the simulator doesn't load, use the observations in the callout below.</p>

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your observation table (try it first!)

| Front | Warm air mass | Cool air mass | Resulting weather |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cold front** | Pushed up steeply and quickly | Moves in fast and wedges underneath, staying near the ground | Tall clouds, heavy showers or thunderstorms right along the front, then cooler and clearing |
| **Warm front** | Slides gently up and over the cold air | Retreats, stays near the ground | Wide area of layered clouds and steady, lighter precipitation ahead of the front |
| **Occluded front** | Lifted completely off the ground, squeezed between two cooler air masses | Cold air catches up and lifts the warm air | Clouds and precipitation, often widespread |
| **Stationary front** | Rises slowly along the boundary | Neither air mass pushes the other out | Clouds and precipitation that can last for days |

**Pattern across all fronts:** The **cool, dry air stays near the surface** every time. The **warm, moist air rises** at the boundary (at three of the four fronts it is clearly pushed up), and **that's where clouds and precipitation form**.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzCheck("bz-check-fronts", "Check: Fronts", [
  {q: "At every front in the simulator, which air mass stays near the ground?",
   options: ["The warm, moist air", "The cold, dry air, because it is denser", "Whichever moves faster", "Neither; both rise"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Cold air is denser, just like in the bottles, so it stays low. Warm, moist air is less dense and rises over or is pushed up by the cold air."},
  {q: "Where does precipitation form in the simulator?",
   options: ["Far away from any front", "Where the two air masses meet and the warm, moist air rises", "Only inside the cold air mass", "Only over the ocean"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Rising warm, moist air is the key. The next model shows why rising air makes clouds."}
])
```

## Model 2: How Water Behaves in the Air {#bz-cups}

In class you put a tall clear cup upside down over a wide cup of tap water and look at the inside of the top cup with a magnifier. The packet has **three experiments**. Run each one virtually.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bzCupExp = Inputs.radio([
  "1. Hot water (How is water vapor different from the rest of the air?)",
  "2. Hot vs. warm vs. cold water (How does water temperature affect the amount of vapor?)",
  "3. Hot water with and without ice on top (How does air temperature affect the state of water?)"
], {value: "1. Hot water (How is water vapor different from the rest of the air?)"})
viewof bzCupTime = Inputs.range([0, 3], {step: 0.25, value: 2, label: "Minutes watched"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const es = T => 6.112 * Math.exp(17.62 * T / (243.12 + T)); // saturation vapor pressure (hPa)
  const exp = +bzCupExp[0];
  const setups = exp === 1 ? [{w: 50, ice: false, name: "Hot water"}] :
    exp === 2 ? [{w: 50, ice: false, name: "Hot (≈50 °C)"}, {w: 30, ice: false, name: "Warm (≈30 °C)"}, {w: 10, ice: false, name: "Cold (≈10 °C)"}] :
    [{w: 50, ice: false, name: "Hot, no ice"}, {w: 50, ice: true, name: "Hot, ice on top"}];
  const room = 22;
  const res = setups.map(s => {
    const tIn = (s.w + room) / 2;            // air trapped inside the cups
    const tTop = s.ice ? 2 : Math.max(room, tIn - 4);  // temperature of the top cup's surface
    const rate = Math.max(0, es(tIn) - es(tTop));
    const vapor = es(s.w);
    return {...s, tIn, tTop, rate, vapor, drops: Math.round(Math.min(60, rate * bzCupTime * 0.55))};
  });
  const W = 120, rnd = d3.randomLcg(0.3);
  const cup = (r, i) => {
    const x0 = i * (W + 14) + 6;
    const vaporDots = d3.range(Math.round(Math.min(26, r.vapor / 5))).map(() => `<circle cx="${(x0 + 22 + rnd() * 76).toFixed(1)}" cy="${(125 + rnd() * 45).toFixed(1)}" r="1.8" fill="#38bdf8" opacity=".7"/>`).join("");
    const drops = d3.range(r.drops).map(() => {
      const onTop = r.ice ? rnd() < 0.75 : rnd() < 0.45;
      const x = onTop ? x0 + 34 + rnd() * 52 : (rnd() < .5 ? x0 + 25 + rnd() * 8 : x0 + 87 + rnd() * 8);
      const y = onTop ? 34 + rnd() * 6 : 42 + rnd() * 120;
      return `<circle cx="${x.toFixed(1)}" cy="${y.toFixed(1)}" r="${(1.6 + rnd() * 1.6).toFixed(1)}" fill="#1d4ed8" opacity=".85"/>`;
    }).join("");
    return `<g>
      <path d="M${x0 + 30},30 L${x0 + 90},30 L${x0 + 98},170 L${x0 + 22},170 Z" fill="rgba(226,232,240,.35)" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <path d="M${x0 + 14},170 L${x0 + 106},170 L${x0 + 98},250 L${x0 + 22},250 Z" fill="rgba(226,232,240,.35)" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <path d="M${x0 + 17},195 L${x0 + 103},195 L${x0 + 98},250 L${x0 + 22},250 Z" fill="${d3.interpolateRgb("#bfdbfe", "#fca5a5")(r.w / 50)}"/>
      ${r.ice ? `<rect x="${x0 + 44}" y="14" width="32" height="16" rx="3" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#0284c7"/><text x="${x0 + 60}" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="#0c4a6e">ice</text>` : ""}
      ${vaporDots}${drops}
      <text x="${x0 + 60}" y="270" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">${r.name}</text>
      <text x="${x0 + 60}" y="284" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#334155">${r.drops} drops</text>
    </g>`;
  };
  const Wt = setups.length * (W + 14) + 6;
  return html`<div class="bz-card">
    <svg viewBox="0 0 ${Wt} 292" width="100%" style="max-width:${Wt * 1.3}px;display:block;margin:auto;" role="img" aria-label="Virtual cup experiment showing water vapor and droplets on the top cup">
      ${res.map(cup).join("")}
    </svg>
    <p style="margin:6px 0 0;font-size:.9em;">Light blue dots: water vapor (invisible in real life). Dark blue dots: liquid droplets that formed on the top cup.</p>
  </div>`;
}
```

<p class="bz-note">How the model works: water evaporates faster from warmer water (it uses real saturation vapor pressures: about 12 hPa at 10 °C, 42 hPa at 30 °C, and 123 hPa at 50 °C). Droplets form where the moist air touches a surface cooler than the air, and form fastest where the surface is coldest (the ice). Drop counts are illustrative, not measurements.</p>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzCheck("bz-check-cups", "Check: The cup experiments", [
  {q: "Experiment 1: How did the tiny drops get onto the inside of the top cup?",
   options: ["They splashed up from the water", "Water evaporated into invisible water vapor, rose with the warm air, and condensed back into liquid on the cooler top cup", "They leaked through the plastic", "They came from the room's air outside the cups"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Water vapor is water as a gas mixed into the air. When it touches a cooler surface, the molecules slow down, stick together, and condense into droplets."},
  {q: "Experiment 2: Which cup had the most droplets, and what does that show?",
   options: ["Cold water; cold water evaporates fastest", "Hot water; warmer water puts more water vapor into the air", "All the same; temperature doesn't matter", "Warm water; it's in the middle"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Warmer water → faster-moving molecules → more escape as vapor (more evaporation) → more water available to condense. Warm oceans and warm air can supply a storm with more moisture."},
  {q: "Experiment 3: The top cup with ice on it got more water. What does that tell you?",
   options: ["Ice adds water to the air", "Cooling water vapor makes it condense into liquid faster; cooler air can't hold as much water vapor as warmer air", "Ice makes evaporation stop completely", "Warm air holds less water than cold air"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "To turn vapor back into liquid faster, cool it. Warm air holds water vapor more effectively than cold air, so when moist air cools, some vapor must condense."}
])
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Model 2 (pp. 18–20)

- **Experiment 1:** observations of the water surface and the top cup. What was happening to the hot water? How did the drops get on the top cup?
- **Experiment 2:** observations for hot, warm, and cold water. What caused the differences? What's the relationship between water in the air and the temperature of the water beneath? What could you do to water vapor to make it become liquid faster?
- **Experiment 3:** diagram both setups (with and without ice). Does cooling water vapor increase the rate it becomes liquid? Does air hold water more effectively at high or low temperatures?
:::

## Making Sense of the Precipitation Formation Investigation {#bz-making-sense-2}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: See-Think-Wonder (pp. 21–22)

Characteristics and movement of the air masses in the fronts simulation; what happened to the warm water and in the top cup; differences with cold, warm, and hot water. For each, *consider what you know about how heating affects matter at the molecular level.*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
From the teacher guide's Look & Listen For:

- Warm, moist air **rises** at three out of the four fronts. Cool, dry air **stays near Earth's surface** at all fronts.
- Precipitation occurs when the two air masses meet and warm, moist air rises, because **warmer air has a lower density** than cooler air.
- When the warm air reaches the top of the container where it's cooler, **water droplets form**: the water vapor **condenses** into liquid when cooled.
- When the water is warmer, **more water evaporates**. Maybe warmer waters cause more rain (and snow) in the atmosphere.
- When the air is cooler, the water vapor turns to liquid.
:::

# Explain 2: Explaining Precipitation Formation {#bz-explain-2}

::: {.explain-box}
## 🧩 From Water Molecules to Snowflakes

In Explain 1 you used **air molecules** to explain wind. Now use **water molecules** to explain clouds, rain, and snow. In class, you'll first review how water changes phase in the **States of Matter** simulator (heated: solid → liquid → gas; cooled: gas → liquid → solid).
:::

## Part 1: The Water Cycle and Cloud Formation {#bz-water-cycle}

In class you watch the video *The Water Cycle* and connect it to the cup lab. Here is a model of a bubble ("parcel") of **warm, moist air** that is pushed up at a front. Air temperature drops with altitude in the troposphere, so the parcel cools as it rises.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bzParcel = Inputs.form({
  T: Inputs.range([30, 80], {step: 1, value: 50, label: "Warm, moist air: temperature at the ground (°F)"}),
  Td: Inputs.range([10, 80], {step: 1, value: 44, label: "Warm, moist air: dew point (°F)"}),
  cold: Inputs.range([0, 50], {step: 1, value: 26, label: "Cold air mass: temperature at the ground (°F)"})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const toC = f => (f - 32) * 5 / 9;
  const T = toC(bzParcel.T), Td = toC(Math.min(bzParcel.Td, bzParcel.T));
  const base = 0.125 * (T - Td);               // km, about 125 m per °C of spread
  const prof = d3.range(0, 8.01, 0.1).map(z => ({z, t: z <= base ? T - 9.8 * z : T - 9.8 * base - 6.0 * (z - base)}));
  const tBase = T - 9.8 * base;
  const freezeZ = tBase <= 0 ? base : base + tBase / 6.0;
  const coldC = toC(bzParcel.cold);
  const snowAtGround = coldC <= 0;
  const precipType = snowAtGround ? "❄️ Snow can reach the ground: the cold air near the surface is at or below 32 °F (0 °C)." : (coldC < 2 ? "🌨️ Mixed rain and snow is likely: the air near the ground is just above freezing." : "🌧️ Snow melts on the way down and falls as rain: the air near the ground is above freezing.");
  const fmtF = c => Math.round(c * 9 / 5 + 32);
  return html`<div class="bz-card">
    ${Plot.plot({
      width: Math.min(width, 560), height: 320, marginLeft: 48,
      x: {label: "Temperature of the rising air (°F)", domain: [-40, 85]},
      y: {label: "Altitude (km)", domain: [0, 8]},
      marks: [
        Plot.rect([{a: base, b: 8}], {x1: () => -40, x2: () => 85, y1: "a", y2: "b", fill: "#cbd5e1", fillOpacity: 0.35}),
        Plot.ruleX([32], {stroke: "#0284c7", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
        Plot.text([{x: 32, y: 7.6}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => "32 °F", dx: 18, fill: "#0369a1", fontSize: 11}),
        Plot.line(prof, {x: d => d.t * 9 / 5 + 32, y: "z", stroke: "#dc2626", strokeWidth: 3}),
        Plot.ruleY([base], {stroke: "#475569"}),
        Plot.text([{x: 84, y: base}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => `cloud base ≈ ${base.toFixed(1)} km`, textAnchor: "end", dy: -7, fontSize: 11, fill: "#334155"}),
        ...(freezeZ < 8 ? [Plot.dot([{x: 32, y: freezeZ}], {x: "x", y: "y", r: 6, fill: "#0ea5e9", stroke: "white"}),
          Plot.text([{x: 32, y: freezeZ}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => `ice crystals above ≈ ${freezeZ.toFixed(1)} km`, textAnchor: "start", dx: 9, fontSize: 11, fill: "#0c4a6e"})] : [])
      ]
    })}
    <ul style="margin:6px 0 0;padding-left:18px;font-size:.93em;">
      <li>The air cools as it rises. At the <b>cloud base (≈ ${base.toFixed(1)} km)</b> it has cooled to its dew point (${fmtF(Td)} °F): water vapor <b>condenses</b> into droplets, and a cloud forms (gray band).</li>
      <li>${freezeZ < 8 ? `Above about <b>${freezeZ.toFixed(1)} km</b> the cloud is below freezing, so water forms <b>ice crystals</b> that grow into snowflakes.` : "The cloud stays above freezing in this range."}</li>
      <li>${precipType}</li>
    </ul>
  </div>`;
}
```

<p class="bz-note">Model rules: rising air cools about 9.8 °C per km before a cloud forms and about 6 °C per km inside the cloud (condensation releases some heat). The cloud base is about 125 m higher for every 1 °C between temperature and dew point. These are standard rule-of-thumb values; real storms are more complicated.</p>

### Your cause and effect storyboard {#bz-storyboard}

The packet's storyboard (p. 24) starts with a **cold, dry air mass** meeting a **warm, moist air mass** and ends with **precipitation**. Tap the steps in the order they happen.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const steps = [
    "A cold, dry air mass meets a warm, moist air mass at a front.",
    "The cold air is denser, so it stays low and wedges under; the warm, moist air is less dense, so it rises.",
    "As the warm, moist air rises, it cools, because temperature drops with altitude in the troposphere.",
    "Cooled water vapor molecules slow down and condense into tiny droplets or ice crystals: a cloud forms.",
    "Droplets and crystals grow until they're heavy enough to fall: precipitation.",
    "If the air is at or below 32 °F (0 °C) all the way down, the precipitation falls as snow."
  ];
  const order = bzOrder("storyboard", steps.length);
  const box = html`<div class="bz-card"></div>`;
  const list = html`<div></div>`, picked = html`<ol style="padding-left:20px;margin:8px 0;"></ol>`;
  const fb = html`<div style="font-size:.92em;min-height:1.3em;"></div>`;
  let next = 0;
  const reset = html`<button class="bz-btn alt">↺ Start over</button>`;
  const build = () => {
    list.innerHTML = ""; picked.innerHTML = ""; next = 0; fb.textContent = "";
    order.forEach(i => {
      const b = html`<button class="bz-opt" style="display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 12px;margin:5px 0;border:2px solid #cbd5e1;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e293b;cursor:pointer;">${steps[i]}</button>`;
      b.onclick = () => {
        if (i === next) {
          b.remove(); picked.append(html`<li style="margin:4px 0;color:#14532d;">${steps[i]}</li>`); next++;
          fb.innerHTML = next === steps.length ? "🎉 That's the full cause-and-effect chain from Explain 2. Draw it in your storyboard boxes!" : "✅ Yes. What happens next?";
        } else {
          b.style.borderColor = "#dc2626";
          fb.textContent = "❌ Not yet. Think: what has to happen before this step can happen?";
          setTimeout(() => { b.style.borderColor = "#cbd5e1"; }, 900);
        }
      };
      list.append(b);
    });
  };
  reset.onclick = build;
  build();
  box.append(html`<div style="font-weight:700;">Your storyboard so far:</div>`, picked, fb, list, reset);
  return box;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔎 Why trust temperature maps from a model?
The teacher guide points out that the packet's temperature maps come from a **computational model built on more than 100 data sets** from research groups around the world, and only data the models **agreed on** was used. When many independent data sets agree, you can be more confident in the result. Models still have **limited reliability**, but agreement among many sources improves it. You'll use this idea again in the Evaluate.
:::

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Explaining Precipitation Formation (pp. 23–26)

- **Part 1:** answer Q1–3 about the video, then draw the **cause and effect storyboard** of how clouds form and why precipitation happens when a cold, dry air mass meets a warm, moist air mass. Annotate every box. (In class, pairs combine their storyboards into a poster that also shows why some precipitation falls as **snow**.)
- **Part 2:** Q1 (two air masses), Q2–3 (summer vs. winter temperatures), Q4 (where else in the world, and when), Q5 (the Arctic desert).
:::

::: {.key-idea}
### 💡 Consensus ideas (Take Time for These Key Points)
- When **warm, moist air** meets **cool, dry air**, the warm, moist air **rises** because it is **less dense**.
- Temperature is **lower** higher in the atmosphere, so the warm, moist air **cools as it rises**, and water molecules **condense** to form **clouds**.
- When the water is heavy enough, it falls as **precipitation**.
- **Warm water → more evaporation** → more water in the atmosphere to form clouds and precipitation.
- **Snow** happens when the air is cold enough to freeze water. That's why blizzards occur during the **winter** at **higher latitudes**.
:::

### Summary Task {#bz-summary-2}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Summary Task (p. 27)

The packet reprints the same three Summary Task questions from p. 16 (molecular-scale mechanisms, energy and matter at two scales, independent vs. dependent variables). This time, answer them about **precipitation**: how clouds form and why precipitation falls as snow.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Summary Task (try it first!)
1. **Molecular scale → precipitation:** Warm water molecules move fast enough to escape as vapor (evaporation). When moist air rises and cools, the vapor molecules slow down and stick together as droplets (condensation). Below 32 °F they lock into ice crystals.
2. **Energy and matter:** *Matter* (water) moves from the ground or ocean to the air (evaporation), up into clouds, and back down as rain or snow. *Energy* is absorbed when water evaporates and released when it condenses, so the rising, cooling air drives the change. Observable scale: clouds, rain, snow, fronts. Molecular scale: molecule speed and spacing.
3. **Variables:** For example, *independent:* temperature of the water/air (how warm and moist the air mass is); *dependent:* the amount of precipitation. The temperature changes the evaporation and precipitation, not the other way around.
:::

```{ojs}
// Inverse-distance-weighted grid + contour lines (as GeoJSON MultiLineStrings in lon/lat).
bzGrid = (pts) => {
  const lon0 = -125, lat0 = 24, step = 0.5, nx = 119, ny = 53;
  const vals = new Float64Array(nx * ny);
  for (let j = 0; j < ny; j++) for (let i = 0; i < nx; i++) {
    const lon = lon0 + i * step, lat = lat0 + j * step;
    let num = 0, den = 0, exact = null;
    for (const p of pts) {
      const dx = (p.lon - lon) * Math.cos(lat * Math.PI / 180), dy = p.lat - lat;
      const d2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;
      if (d2 < 1e-6) { exact = p.v; break; }
      const w = 1 / (d2 * d2);
      num += w * p.v; den += w;
    }
    vals[i + j * nx] = exact ?? num / den;
  }
  const at = (lon, lat) => {
    const i = Math.max(0, Math.min(nx - 1, Math.round((lon - lon0) / step))), j = Math.max(0, Math.min(ny - 1, Math.round((lat - lat0) / step)));
    return vals[i + j * nx];
  };
  const lines = (thresholds) => d3.contours().size([nx, ny]).thresholds(thresholds)(vals).map(c => {
    const segs = [];
    for (const poly of c.coordinates) for (const ring of poly) {
      let cur = [];
      for (const [x, y] of ring) {
        const edge = x <= 0.01 || y <= 0.01 || x >= nx - 0.01 || y >= ny - 0.01;
        if (edge) { if (cur.length > 1) segs.push(cur); cur = []; }
        else cur.push([lon0 + (x - 0.5) * step, lat0 + (y - 0.5) * step]);
      }
      if (cur.length > 1) segs.push(cur);
    }
    return {value: c.value, geo: {type: "MultiLineString", coordinates: segs}, segs};
  }).filter(c => c.segs.length);
  return {vals, at, lines, nx, ny, lon0, lat0, step};
}
bzGridP = bzGrid(bzPres)
bzGridT = bzGrid(bzTemp)
bzGridD = bzGrid(bzDP)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bzMapPick = Inputs.select(["1. Air Pressure Map (isobars)", "2. Temperature Map (isotherms)", "4. Air Pressure Change Map (isallobars)"], {label: "Map:"})
viewof bzMapShow = Inputs.checkbox(["Isolines", "Shading", "H and L", "Wind arrows"], {label: "Show:", value: []})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const k = +bzMapPick[0];
  const pts = k === 1 ? bzPres : k === 2 ? bzTemp : bzDP;
  const G = k === 1 ? bzGridP : k === 2 ? bzGridT : bzGridD;
  const thr = k === 1 ? d3.range(1008, 1025, 4) : k === 2 ? d3.range(20, 91, 10) : d3.range(-6, 7, 2);
  const show = new Set(bzMapShow);
  const memo = new Map();
  const inside = (lon, lat) => {
    if (!bzUS) return true;
    const key = lon.toFixed(2) + "," + lat.toFixed(2);
    if (!memo.has(key)) memo.set(key, d3.geoContains(bzUS.nation, [lon, lat]));
    return memo.get(key);
  };
  // keep only the parts of each isoline that are inside the U.S.
  // nudge the lowest and highest isolines slightly inward so they enclose the stations with exactly that value
  const thrAdj = thr.map((v, i) => i === 0 ? v + 0.4 : i === thr.length - 1 ? v - 0.4 : v);
  const lines = (show.has("Isolines") ? G.lines(thrAdj) : []).map(c => {
    const segs = [];
    for (const seg of c.segs) {
      let cur = [];
      for (const p of seg) { if (inside(p[0], p[1])) cur.push(p); else { if (cur.length > 1) segs.push(cur); cur = []; } }
      if (cur.length > 1) segs.push(cur);
    }
    return {value: thr[thrAdj.indexOf(c.value)], segs, geo: {type: "MultiLineString", coordinates: segs}};
  }).filter(c => c.segs.length);
  const lab = v => k === 1 ? String(v).slice(-2) : k === 4 ? (v > 0 ? "+" + v : String(v)) : String(v);
  const labels = lines.map(c => {
    const seg = c.segs.reduce((a, b) => b.length > a.length ? b : a);
    const pt = seg[Math.floor(seg.length / 2)];
    return {lon: pt[0], lat: pt[1], t: lab(c.value)};
  });
  // shading
  let shade = [];
  if (show.has("Shading") && k !== 1) {
    for (let lon = -124.5; lon <= -67; lon += 1) for (let lat = 25; lat <= 49; lat += 1) {
      if (!inside(lon, lat)) continue;
      const v = G.at(lon, lat);
      const c = k === 2 ? (v <= 25 ? "#3b82f6" : v >= 70 ? "#ef4444" : null) : (v <= -4 ? "#ef4444" : v >= 4 ? "#3b82f6" : null);
      if (c) shade.push({lon, lat, c});
    }
  }
  // wind arrows (pressure map only): clockwise around H, counterclockwise around L, turned slightly toward low pressure
  let vecs = [];
  if (show.has("Wind arrows") && k === 1) {
    for (let lon = -122; lon <= -70; lon += 3.5) for (let lat = 27; lat <= 48; lat += 3) {
      if (!inside(lon, lat)) continue;
      const c = Math.cos(lat * Math.PI / 180);
      const gx = (G.at(lon + 0.5, lat) - G.at(lon - 0.5, lat)) / (1 * c), gy = (G.at(lon, lat + 0.5) - G.at(lon, lat - 0.5)) / 1;
      const mag = Math.hypot(gx, gy); if (mag < 0.3) continue;
      const u = -gy - 0.45 * gx, v = gx - 0.45 * gy;
      vecs.push({lon, lat, rot: Math.atan2(u, v) * 180 / Math.PI, len: Math.min(22, 8 + 3 * mag)});
    }
  }
  const HL = k === 1 && show.has("H and L") ? [{lon: -109.3, lat: 40.4, t: "H", c: "#1d4ed8"}, {lon: -86.2, lat: 38.8, t: "L", c: "#dc2626"}] : [];
  const w = Math.min(width, 720);
  const lineColor = k === 1 ? "#111827" : k === 2 ? "#1d4ed8" : "#7c3aed";
  return Plot.plot({
    title: ["1. Air Pressure Map (mb)", "2. Temperature Map (°F)", "", "4. Air Pressure Change Map (mb in the past 3 hours)"][k - 1],
    subtitle: show.has("Isolines") ? (k === 1 ? "Isobars every 4 mb, labeled with the last two digits" : k === 2 ? "Isotherms every 10 °F" : "Isallobars every 2 mb") : "Station values from the packet. Turn on isolines to check your drawing.",
    width: w, height: w * 0.62,
    projection: bzUS ? {type: "albers-usa", domain: bzUS.nation} : {type: "equirectangular", domain: {type: "MultiPoint", coordinates: [[-125, 24], [-66, 50]]}},
    marks: [
      bzUS ? Plot.geo(bzUS.states, {fill: "#f8fafc", stroke: "#cbd5e1", strokeWidth: 0.7}) : Plot.graticule({strokeOpacity: 0.25}),
      Plot.dot(shade, {x: "lon", y: "lat", fill: "c", r: w / 70, symbol: "square", fillOpacity: 0.28}),
      ...lines.map(c => Plot.geo(c.geo, {stroke: lineColor, strokeWidth: 1.6})),
      Plot.text(labels, {x: "lon", y: "lat", text: "t", fontSize: 11, fontWeight: "bold", fill: lineColor, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 4}),
      Plot.vector(vecs, {x: "lon", y: "lat", rotate: "rot", length: "len", stroke: "#0f766e", strokeWidth: 1.6, anchor: "middle"}),
      Plot.text(pts, {x: "lon", y: "lat", text: d => k === 4 && d.v > 0 ? "+" + d.v : String(d.v), fontSize: 10, fill: "#111827", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.text(HL, {x: "lon", y: "lat", text: "t", fontSize: 34, fontWeight: "bold", fill: "c", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3})
    ]
  });
}
```

<p class="bz-note">Isolines here are drawn by a computer that estimates values between stations (inverse-distance interpolation), so they may look a little different from a hand drawing. "H and L" and "Wind arrows" work on the Air Pressure Map; "Shading" works on the Temperature and Pressure Change maps (temperature: blue ≤ 25 °F, red ≥ 70 °F; pressure change: red ≤ −4 mb, blue ≥ +4 mb).</p>

### 3. Dew Point Map {#bz-dewpoint}

The **dew point** is the temperature air would have to cool to for it to be completely **saturated** (holding all the water vapor it can). On the packet's dew point map, you connect equal dew points every 10 °F (**isodrosotherms**, in green). The packet's map shows **low dew points (around 5–20 °F) in the northern Plains and Rockies** and **high dew points (60–70 °F) along the Gulf Coast and Southeast**.

- The **closer** the temperature and dew point, the **more moisture** in the air and the greater the chance of precipitation.
- **Moist air is lighter (less dense) than dry air**, so it lifts more easily, which helps thunderstorms form. Dew points of **70 °F or more** have the potential energy for severe weather.

```{ojs}

   correct: 0,

])
```

## Analyzing a Complete Surface Observation Map {#bz-surface-obs}

Weather stations at airports record temperature, dew point, cloud cover, visibility, precipitation, wind speed and direction, and more **every hour**. To fit all of that on a map, each station's data is coded into a **station model**. Build one below (the symbols follow the *Key to Weather Map Symbols*, ESRT p. 13).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzStationSVG = (o) => {
  const cx = 150, cy = 105, r = 13;
  const dirDeg = {N: 0, NE: 45, E: 90, SE: 135, S: 180, SW: 225, W: 270, NW: 315}[o.dir];
  const rad = dirDeg * Math.PI / 180;
  const ex = (d) => [cx + Math.sin(rad) * d, cy - Math.cos(rad) * d];
  const [x1, y1] = ex(r), [x2, y2] = ex(r + 62);
  let kt = Math.round(o.kt / 5) * 5, barbs = "", pos = 0;
  const barbAt = (d, len) => { const [bx, by] = ex(r + 62 - d); const a = rad + Math.PI / 2.6; return `<line x1="${bx}" y1="${by}" x2="${bx + Math.sin(a) * len}" y2="${by - Math.cos(a) * len}" stroke="#111" stroke-width="2"/>`; };
  if (o.kt > 0) {
    while (kt >= 50) { const [ax, ay] = ex(r + 62 - pos), [bx, by] = ex(r + 62 - pos - 10); const a = rad + Math.PI / 2.6; barbs += `<polygon points="${ax},${ay} ${bx},${by} ${ax + Math.sin(a) * 18},${ay - Math.cos(a) * 18}" fill="#111"/>`; pos += 12; kt -= 50; }
    while (kt >= 10) { barbs += barbAt(pos, 18); pos += 8; kt -= 10; }
    if (kt >= 5) { barbs += barbAt(pos === 0 ? 8 : pos, 9); }
  }
  const cover = o.cover;
  const pie = cover === 0 ? "" : cover === 100 ? `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${r}" fill="#111"/>` :
    (() => { const ang = 2 * Math.PI * cover / 100; const xe = cx + r * Math.sin(ang), ye = cy - r * Math.cos(ang); return `<path d="M${cx},${cy} L${cx},${cy - r} A${r},${r} 0 ${cover > 50 ? 1 : 0},1 ${xe},${ye} Z" fill="#111"/>`; })();
  const code = String(Math.round(o.mb * 10) % 1000).padStart(3, "0");
  const wx = {"Snow": "✱✱", "Rain": "••", "Drizzle": ",,", "Fog": "≡", "Thunderstorm": "⚡", "None": ""}[o.wx];
  const vis = o.vis === 0.25 ? "¼" : o.vis === 0.5 ? "½" : String(o.vis);
  return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 300 200" width="100%" style="max-width:380px;display:block;margin:auto;background:#fff;border-radius:10px;" role="img" aria-label="Station model">
    <circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${r}" fill="#fff" stroke="#111" stroke-width="2"/>${pie}
    ${o.kt > 0 ? `<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="#111" stroke-width="2"/>${barbs}` : `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${r + 5}" fill="none" stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.5"/>`}
    <text x="${cx - 24}" y="${cy - 14}" text-anchor="end" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#111">${o.T}</text>
    <text x="${cx - 24}" y="${cy + 32}" text-anchor="end" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#111">${o.Td}</text>
    <text x="${cx - 22}" y="${cy + 7}" text-anchor="end" font-size="17" fill="#111">${wx}</text>
    <text x="${cx - (wx ? 52 : 26)}" y="${cy + 7}" text-anchor="end" font-size="17" fill="#111">${vis}</text>
    <text x="${cx + 24}" y="${cy - 14}" text-anchor="start" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#111">${code}</text>
    
  </svg>`;
}
viewof bzSM = Inputs.form({
  T: Inputs.range([-20, 100], {step: 1, value: 57, label: "Temperature (°F)"}),
  Td: Inputs.range([-30, 80], {step: 1, value: 56, label: "Dew point (°F)"}),
  mb: Inputs.range([960, 1050], {step: 0.1, value: 1010.7, label: "Sea-level pressure (mb)"}),
  dir: Inputs.select(["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"], {value: "SW", label: "Wind FROM"}),
  kt: Inputs.range([0, 70], {step: 5, value: 15, label: "Wind speed (knots)"}),
  cover: Inputs.select([0, 25, 50, 75, 100], {value: 100, label: "Sky cover (%)"}),
  wx: Inputs.select(["None", "Rain", "Drizzle", "Snow", "Fog", "Thunderstorm"], {value: "Drizzle", label: "Present weather"}),
  vis: Inputs.select([0.25, 0.5, 1, 3, 5, 10], {value: 3, label: "Visibility (miles)"})
})
```

```{ojs}
<p style="font-size:.9em;margin:8px 0 0;">Coded pressure: drop the first 9 or 10 and the decimal point. ${bzSM.mb.toFixed(1)} mb → <b>${String(Math.round(bzSM.mb * 10) % 1000).padStart(3, "0")}</b>. To decode, put a 9 in front if the code is 500 or more, or a 10 if it's less, then put back the decimal (e.g., 107 → 1010.7 mb; 872 → 987.2 mb). The wind staff points to the direction the wind blows <b>from</b>; each full barb = 10 knots, half barb = 5, triangle = 50.</p></div>`
```

### Drawing the fronts {#bz-fronts-map}

On a weather map, fronts are drawn where there are **large changes in temperature**, changes in **wind direction and speed**, and large changes in **pressure**. Use the station models around the L to draw a **cold front (blue)** and a **warm front (red)**. Hint: look where isotherms are crowded and pressure changes most, passing through the low.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzCheck("bz-check-fronts-map", "Check: Fronts on the surface map", [
  {q: "Compare the pressure change on each side of the cold front. What do you observe?",
   options: ["Pressure is rising behind the cold front (cold, dense air arriving) and falling ahead of it", "Pressure is the same on both sides", "Pressure falls behind the cold front", "Cold fronts have no effect on pressure"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "On the packet's pressure change map, rising values (+3 to +6) are behind the front to the west and falling values (−3 to −5) are ahead of it to the east."},
  {q: "What do you notice about cloud cover and precipitation near the cold and warm fronts?",
   options: ["Skies are cloudy (shaded circles) and precipitation symbols appear along and near the fronts", "Skies are clear at the fronts", "Precipitation is only found at the high", "There are no clouds anywhere"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Fronts are where warm, moist air is forced to rise. That's exactly what your Explain 2 model predicts."}
])
```

As the warm air rises it cools, its water vapor condenses into tall clouds, and you get a burst of heavy precipitation, then colder weather", "Warm air pushes cold air out of the way and it gets warmer", "Nothing happens at cold fronts", "Cold air rises over warm air"],
```{ojs}
   correct: 0,
```

```{ojs}
])
```

**The mid-latitude cyclone.** Jonas was a **mid-latitude cyclone**: a large low-pressure system with a cold front and a warm front. This diagram matches the one on p. 40.

### Air masses {#bz-air-masses}

An **air mass** is a large body of air with similar **temperature** and **humidity (moisture)**. The two-letter codes come from where the air mass formed.

::: {.bz-scroll}

| Air mass | Humidity | Temperature | Forms over |
|---|---|---|---|
| **cA** continental arctic | Dry | Very cold | Arctic land (northern Canada, Alaska) |
| **cP** continental polar | Dry | Cold | Canada |
| **mP** maritime polar | Wet | Cold | North Pacific and North Atlantic |
| **mT** maritime tropical | Wet | Warm | Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean, subtropical Atlantic and Pacific |
| **cT** continental tropical | Dry | Warm | Deserts of Mexico and the U.S. Southwest |

:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const items = [["I. Continental", "over land (dry)"], ["II. Maritime", "over the sea (moist)"], ["III. Arctic", "extremely cold"], ["IV. Polar", "cold"], ["V. Tropical", "warm/hot"], ["VI. Continental Polar (cP)", "cold and dry"], ["VII. Maritime Tropical (mT)", "warm and moist"]];
  const opts = ["(choose)", "warm/hot", "extremely cold", "cold and dry", "over land (dry)", "cold", "warm and moist", "over the sea (moist)"];
  const box = html`<div class="bz-card"><div style="font-weight:700;margin-bottom:6px;">Match each term with its description (p. 41 Q4)</div></div>`;
  const sels = items.map(([term]) => { const l = html`<label style="display:block;margin:6px 0;font-weight:600;">${term}<br><select style="width:100%;border:2px solid #cbd5e1;border-radius:8px;padding:6px;background:#fff;color:#1a1a1a;">${opts.map(o => html`<option>${o}</option>`)}</select></label>`; box.append(l); return l.querySelector("select"); });
  const fb = html`<div style="font-size:.92em;margin-top:6px;"></div>`;
  const btn = html`<button class="bz-btn">Check my matches</button>`;
  btn.onclick = () => { let n = 0; sels.forEach((s, i) => { const ok = s.value === items[i][1]; s.style.borderColor = ok ? "#16a34a" : "#dc2626"; if (ok) n++; }); fb.textContent = n === 7 ? "✅ All 7 correct! For Jonas, think cold, dry cP/cA air from Canada meeting warm, moist mT air from the Gulf and Atlantic." : `${n} of 7 correct. Continental/maritime = where it formed (land or sea); arctic/polar/tropical = how cold or warm.`; };
  box.append(btn, fb);
  return box;
}
```

## 🔮 Can We Predict Future Blizzards?

## Part 1: Are winter storms becoming more frequent and stronger? {#bz-future-1}

The packet's graphs show winter storm **frequency** (how many) and **intensity** (how strong) during the cold season (**November–March**) for each decade from the **1950s to the 2000s**, for the Northern Hemisphere's **high latitudes** (60–90° N) and **mid-latitudes** (30–60° N, where NYC is). Each bar is how much more (+) or less (−) than the long-term average that decade was.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzNCA = {
  const dec = [1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000];
  const s = {
    "High-latitudes|Frequency": [-1.05, -0.25, -0.15, 0.55, 0.45, 0.55],
    "High-latitudes|Intensity": [-0.52, -0.65, -0.03, 0.18, 0.78, 0.28],
    "Mid-latitudes|Frequency": [-1.13, 0.25, -0.03, 0.15, -0.37, 1.12],
    "Mid-latitudes|Intensity": [-1.23, -0.10, 0.02, 0.31, 0.16, 0.86]
  };
  return Object.entries(s).flatMap(([k, v]) => { const [region, measure] = k.split("|"); return v.map((y, i) => ({region, measure, decade: dec[i], label: dec[i] + "s", y})); });
}
viewof bzNCAregion = Inputs.radio(["Mid-latitudes", "High-latitudes"], {value: "Mid-latitudes", label: "Region:"})
```

## Part 2: Using Climate Models to Make Predictions About the Future {#bz-future-2}

**Reviewing what we know about blizzard formation** (from Explain 1 and Explain 2, Part 2):

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your review answers (try it first!)
1. **Two key elements of a winter storm:** strong **wind** and heavy **precipitation (snow)**.
2. **What's required:** wind needs **differences in air pressure**, made by **uneven heating** (warm and cold air masses). Snow needs a **warm, moist air mass** meeting a **cold air mass** at a front (so moist air rises, cools, and condenses), plus air **at or below 32 °F** so the precipitation falls as snow.
3. **Where and when:** in the **mid- and high-latitudes**, during **winter** (November–April in the Northern Hemisphere), where cold polar air meets warm, moist air, as in **mid-latitude cyclones** like Jonas.
:::

### Analyzing data from a climate model: IPCC WGI Interactive Atlas {#bz-ipcc}

In class you open the [IPCC WGI Interactive Atlas](https://interactive-atlas.ipcc.ch/){target="_blank"}, choose a **custom season** (like **November to April**), click the regions where blizzards form (for NYC: **Eastern North America**), and look at the line graph of **mean temperature** and other variables (try **precipitation**). Every projection shows the cold season **warming**, with the most warming at high latitudes.

What could a few degrees of warming mean for NYC's winters? This **what-if model** uses real NYC daily temperatures (Central Park, December–March, 1991–2020) and simply adds the same warming to every day.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzFreeze = [
  {dF: 0, mean: 28.3, max: 13.1}, {dF: 1, mean: 25.3, max: 10.6}, {dF: 2, mean: 22.2, max: 8.9}, {dF: 3, mean: 19.4, max: 7.3},
  {dF: 4, mean: 16.9, max: 6.0}, {dF: 5, mean: 14.5, max: 5.2}, {dF: 6, mean: 12.4, max: 4.2}, {dF: 7, mean: 10.2, max: 3.6},
  {dF: 8, mean: 8.6, max: 3.0}, {dF: 9, mean: 6.8, max: 2.5}, {dF: 10, mean: 5.8, max: 2.1}
]
viewof bzWarm = Inputs.range([0, 10], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "Winter warming (°F)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const row = bzFreeze[bzWarm];
  return html`<div>${Plot.plot({
    title: "Share of NYC winter days (Dec–Mar) at or below freezing",
    subtitle: "Real 1991–2020 Central Park days (NOAA) shifted warmer. Shaded bands: NYC Panel on Climate Change (2019) middle-range projections for the 2050s and 2080s",
    width, height: 280, marginLeft: 44,
    x: {label: "Warming added (°F)", domain: [0, 10]},
    y: {label: "% of winter days", domain: [0, 30], grid: true},
    color: {domain: ["Daily mean ≤ 32 °F", "Whole day below freezing (high ≤ 32 °F)"], range: ["#1d4ed8", "#0891b2"], legend: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.rect([{a: 4.1, b: 5.7, t: "2050s"}, {a: 5.3, b: 8.8, t: "2080s"}], {x1: "a", x2: "b", y1: () => 0, y2: () => 30, fill: d => d.t === "2050s" ? "#fde68a" : "#fecaca", fillOpacity: 0.35}),
      Plot.text([{x: 4.9, t: "2050s"}, {x: 7.05, t: "2080s"}], {x: "x", y: () => 28.5, text: "t", fontSize: 10, fill: "#7c2d12"}),
      Plot.line(bzFreeze, {x: "dF", y: "mean", stroke: () => "Daily mean ≤ 32 °F", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.line(bzFreeze, {x: "dF", y: "max", stroke: () => "Whole day below freezing (high ≤ 32 °F)", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot([row], {x: "dF", y: "mean", r: 6, fill: "#1d4ed8", stroke: "white"}),
      Plot.dot([row], {x: "dF", y: "max", r: 6, fill: "#0891b2", stroke: "white"})
    ]
  })}<p style="margin:4px 0 0;font-weight:600;">+${bzWarm} °F: ${row.mean}% of winter days average at or below freezing (now 28.3%); ${row.max}% stay below freezing all day (now 13.1%).</p></div>`;
}
```

<p class="bz-note">The NPCC (2019) projects NYC's average temperature to rise about 4.1–5.7 °F by the 2050s and 5.3–8.8 °F by the 2080s (middle range), and winter precipitation to increase. This model ignores changes in storms, moisture, and variability, which is exactly the kind of assumption that limits a prediction's precision. See also [Unit 4: The Past and the Future](../unit4-climate-change/unit4-past-and-future.qmd).</p>

```{ojs}

   options: ["It drops from about 28% to about 15%: roughly half as many cold days for snow", "It doubles", "It stays the same", "It goes to zero"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Fewer freezing days means more storms could bring rain instead of snow. That's evidence a frequency claim might be 'decrease.'"},
  {q: "Warmer air and oceans also mean more evaporation. How could that affect the storms that DO happen when it's cold enough to snow?",

])
```

### Evaluating precision and accuracy of models {#bz-precision}

**Precision** asks whether a model gives **consistent, dependable** results. The packet's example: a scale that shows **100 grams** every time you weigh the same 100-gram apple is precise. Having **several scales that all agree** makes you even more confident.

The IPCC Atlas does the same thing with climate: each line on its graph combines **many climate models** (the Atlas shows the number of models, often 30 or more), each built by a different research group. When many models built in different ways agree, the projection is more dependable. Where the models **spread apart**, the prediction is less precise.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bzCheck("bz-check-precision", "Check: Precision (p. 45)", [
  {q: "Why does basing the Atlas on many models enhance its precision?",
   options: ["When many independent models agree, the result is consistent and less likely to be an error of one model, like several scales all reading 100 g", "More models always give the exact future temperature", "Only one model is ever used", "More models make the result less certain"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Agreement across many models (and many data sets) raises confidence. The spread between models shows how much uncertainty remains."},
  {q: "Which prediction is the climate models MORE confident about?",
   options: ["That winter temperatures will rise", "Exactly how many blizzards NYC will have in 2075", "The date of the next blizzard", "That storms will stop forming"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Temperature projections agree well across models. Storm counts for one city depend on many more factors (storm tracks, moisture, variability), so they're much less precise. Keep that in mind for your counterclaim."}
])
```
