## 🔗 Connect to the Performance Task: Blizzards 5E {#bz-pt}

In your **Performance Task Organizer** (pp. 9–14), *"Choose one of the two tasks below and apply what you figured out from the Blizzards 5E to complete the task."*

> **Task 1:** *"Will the **frequency** of winter storms per year where you live increase, decrease, or stay the same as global temperatures increase in the future?"*
>
> **Task 2:** *"Will the **intensity** of winter storms where you live increase, decrease, or stay the same as global temperatures increase in the future?"*

Each task has three parts: **Part 1** identify the independent and dependent variables; **Part 2** gather evidence in a table (*What is the evidence? Which resource did it come from?*) and develop a model showing *how and why energy and matter flow within the storm system* and *small scale mechanisms that explain what you are representing at the macro scale*; **Part 3** argue from evidence with a **claim** and a **counterclaim**, considering historical data, the conditions needed for a winter storm (or for intense snowfall), climate model projections, and the precision and reliability of the models.

<p class="bz-note">Tip from the teacher guide: the <b>intensity</b> task (Task 2) is often more accessible, because the evidence lines up. Frequency evidence points in different directions, so a strong Task 1 answer weighs the competing evidence and may conclude we can't be sure. (Note: the teacher guide's materials list names "Connect to the Performance Task: Hurricanes 5E" here; the PTO's Blizzards 5E pages are the right ones.)</p>

**Still to figure out:** we know how winter storms form, but not yet **where they go**. Will warming change the **paths** of storms like Jonas? That's next: [Paths of Severe Storms](unit5-storm-paths.qmd). Then we'll ask the same questions about [Hurricanes](unit5-hurricanes.qmd).

# Chapter Summary {#bz-chapter-summary}

| Key Concept | Details |
|---|---|
| **Wind** | Air moving horizontally across Earth's surface, from **high to low pressure** |
| **Heating and density** | Heated air molecules speed up and spread apart (less dense, rise); cooled molecules slow and crowd together (denser, sink) |
| **High and low pressure** | Cool, sinking air → **high** pressure at the surface (dry, clear). Warm, rising air → **low** pressure (clouds, precipitation) |
| **Cause and effect** | Bigger temperature difference → bigger pressure difference → stronger wind. Independent variable: temperature difference; dependent: wind |
| **Air masses and fronts** | Air masses have similar temperature and moisture (cA, cP, mP, mT, cT). At fronts, cold dense air stays low and warm, moist air rises |
| **Clouds and precipitation** | Rising air cools; water vapor condenses into droplets or ice; heavy drops fall. Warmer water → more evaporation → more water for storms |
| **Snow and blizzards** | Need cold air (≤ 32 °F), moisture, and a front; occur in mid- and high latitudes in winter (Nov–Apr in the Northern Hemisphere) |
| **Weather maps** | Isobars (pressure, every 4 mb), isotherms (temperature), isodrosotherms (dew point), isallobars (pressure change). Wind circles clockwise out of H, counterclockwise into L |
| **Mid-latitude cyclone** | A low with a cold front (blue triangles) and warm front (red half circles); Jonas formed over Texas on Jan 21, 2016 and hit NYC Jan 23 with 27.5″ of snow |
| **Future of winter storms** | Since 1950, cold-season storm **intensity** has risen; **frequency** changes are mixed. Warming means fewer freezing days but more moisture, so fewer but possibly more intense snowstorms |
| **Model precision** | Many models and data sets that agree → more confidence; assumptions and approximations limit precision |

```{=html}
    {text: "Warm air rises because it is less dense than the cooler air around it.", type: "Fact",

    {text: "Low-pressure systems usually bring clear, dry weather.", type: "Myth",

    {text: "In the Northern Hemisphere, winds spiral counterclockwise into a low-pressure center.", type: "Fact",
     explanation: "Air flows toward the low, but Earth's rotation turns it. In the Southern Hemisphere the spin is reversed (clockwise)."},
```

```{ojs}
      btn.className = "bz-opt";
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true"; nDone++;
        card.querySelectorAll("button").forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; b.style.color = "#475569"; b.style.background = "#f8fafc"; });
        const right = card.querySelectorAll("button")[shownCorrect];
        right.style.borderColor = "#48bb78"; right.style.background = "#f0fff4"; right.style.color = "#276749"; right.style.fontWeight = "700";
        if (oi === shownCorrect) { nRight++; fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#276749"; fb.style.background = "#f0fff4"; }
        else { btn.style.borderColor = "#fc8181"; btn.style.background = "#fff5f5"; btn.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; btn.style.fontWeight = "700"; fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; fb.style.background = "#fff5f5"; }
        fb.style.padding = "10px 14px"; fb.style.marginTop = "8px";
        scoreEl.textContent = `Score: ${nRight} / ${nDone}`;
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  outer.appendChild(header);
  outer.appendChild(body);
  return outer;
}
```

```{ojs}
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Cool, dense, sinking air makes high pressure; warm, rising air makes low pressure; the horizontal flow from H to L is wind."},
  {q: "In the diffusion model, the left side has 200 particles at 250 K and the right has 50 at 300 K. When the divider is removed, what happens?",

   correct: 1,

  {q: "Two places have a 5 °C temperature difference on Monday and a 25 °C difference on Tuesday. On which day do you predict stronger wind between them, and why?",
   options: ["Monday; smaller differences make more wind", "Tuesday; a bigger temperature difference makes a bigger pressure difference, which drives faster air movement", "Same both days", "You can't predict wind from temperature"],
   correct: 1,

  {q: "In the cup lab, the top cup with ice on it collected the most water. Which part of a storm does this model?",
   options: ["Warm, moist air rising, cooling, and condensing into clouds", "Wind blowing from high to low", "Snow melting on the ground", "Air sinking at a high"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "The cold top acts like the cold upper troposphere: cooling water vapor makes it condense faster."},
  {q: "A weather map shows a closed 1008 mb isobar over Kentucky and a closed 1024 mb isobar over Utah. Where are clouds and precipitation most likely?",
   options: ["Over Utah", "Around Kentucky and the Ohio Valley, near the low", "Exactly halfway between", "Nowhere"],

  {q: "On a surface map, pressure is rising by +5 mb behind a boundary and falling by −4 mb ahead of it, with temperatures dropping sharply behind it. What is the boundary?",
   options: ["A warm front", "A cold front: cold, dense air arriving raises the pressure", "A high-pressure center", "A stationary front with no change"],
   correct: 1,
```
